title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Manufacturing Sector (UK manufacturers, engineering, food and drink production, metals, plastics, textiles, industrial and specialist producers)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency in UK manufacturing 2023-2026 - energy-intensive production hit by the energy price shock, raw material and input cost inflation, supply-chain disruption and longer lead times, post-Brexit export friction and customs cost, weak order books, heavy capital tied up in plant and machinery on finance, and long customer payment terms squeezing working capital? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK manufacturing, engineering or industrial production companies that entered administration, CVL or other insolvency between 2023 and 2026 - company name, month/year, procedure, sub-sector, and stated cause. Verify from London Gazette, insolvency notices, or trade press (The Manufacturer, Insider Media, Made in). Include food and drink producers, metals/foundries, and engineering firms.

How do UK manufacturers appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm they sit in SIC section C (manufacturing), divisions 10-33. Note manufacturing is one of the larger insolvency sections and the Insolvency Service reports at section level for England and Wales; figures are England and Wales only and can be attributed directly to the manufacturing sector.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK manufacturer is heading toward insolvency - margins that no longer cover energy and materials, a shrinking or concentrated order book, stretched supplier and HMRC payment, machinery finance under strain, stock and work-in-progress tying up cash, and a major customer delaying or lost? Frame as indicators, not proof.

What insolvency and rescue options apply to UK manufacturing companies specifically, and what sector complexities arise - the treatment of plant, machinery and tooling on hire purchase or lease and retention-of-title claims by material suppliers, work-in-progress and part-finished orders, warranty and long-term supply contract obligations, TUPE and skilled-workforce retention, pension scheme liabilities, and when administration and a going-concern or pre-pack sale versus a CVL is realistic? Moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.

title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Energy Sector (UK energy suppliers, electricity and gas retailers, renewable generators, energy services and green-tech companies)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency in the UK energy sector 2023-2026 - the 2021-2022 wholesale gas price shock that collapsed dozens of domestic energy suppliers, the price cap squeezing supplier margins, hedging and collateral (credit cover) requirements, undercapitalised supplier business models, and distress among renewable generators, EV-charging and green-tech companies reliant on subsidy and cheap capital? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK energy companies that failed between 2021 and 2026 - domestic energy suppliers, and any electricity/gas or green-tech companies - with company name, month/year, procedure or Supplier of Last Resort transfer, and stated cause. Verify from Ofgem announcements, London Gazette, insolvency notices, or trade press (Utility Week, Current News). Include notable domestic supplier failures and the Bulb special administration.

How do UK energy suppliers and generators appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm electricity and gas businesses sit in SIC section D (electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply), division 35. Note section D is a very small, low-volume insolvency category, so official statistics understate sector distress and the named failures and the Ofgem regime are more informative; the Insolvency Service reports at section level for England and Wales only.

How does the Ofgem Supplier of Last Resort (SoLR) mechanism work when a UK domestic energy supplier fails, and what is special administration for energy - explain how Ofgem appoints another supplier to take on customers and honour credit balances, how the costs are mutualised across the industry and recovered from consumers, when the Special Administration Regime (as used for Bulb) is used instead for very large suppliers, and how this differs from an ordinary company insolvency. Cite Ofgem sources.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK energy supplier or energy company is heading toward insolvency, and what insolvency and rescue options and sector complexities apply - inadequate hedging and margin calls, breaching Ofgem financial-resilience and capital requirements, misuse of customer credit balances and Renewables Obligation payments, and how customer protections, licence conditions and the SoLR/special-administration regimes interact with ordinary administration or CVL for licensed and unlicensed energy businesses? Frame warning signs as indicators, not proof, and moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.
